# One Small Step: The CSLCA and Article II of the Outer Space Treaty

## Citation

Blount, P. J., & Robison, C. J. (2016). One small step: The impact of the U.S. Commercial
Space Launch Competitiveness Act of 2015 on the exploitation of resources in outer space.
*North Carolina Journal of Law & Technology*, *18*(2), 160–186.
https://scholarship.law.unc.edu/ncjolt/vol18/iss2/1

Publisher URL: https://scholarship.law.unc.edu/ncjolt/vol18/iss2/1

**Note on the 2016/2018 date discrepancy:** The PDF's cover sheet (generated by the
repository) lists a deposit date of "12-1-2016" and a Recommended Citation reading "18
N.C. J.L. & TECH. 160 (2018)." The article itself, however, is internally dated
throughout: the running head on every page reads "DEC 2016," the masthead states "VOLUME

relative to a November 2016 NASA plaque citation. No content in the body references events
after 2016. The weight of the internal evidence therefore points to a December 2016

appears to be an error (possibly a repository indexing or reprint artifact) rather than a
feature of the article. This summary cites the source as 2016 per the document's own
internal dating; the discrepancy is flagged here for the compiler to confirm or correct.

**Note on title wording and author name spelling:** The article's own title page (PDF p. 2)
and running head (p. 3) print the title's key term as "exploitation" ("...on the
Exploitation of Resources in Outer Space") and the second author's surname as "Robison."

## Abstract

Law-review article analyzing Title IV of the U.S. Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness
Act of 2015 (CSLCA), which recognizes U.S. citizens' rights to possess, own, transport,
use, and sell space resources they recover. Surveys the ambiguities of Article II of the
1967 Outer Space Treaty, whose non-appropriation clause bars claims of sovereignty over
outer space through use, occupation, or any comparable means, across three dimensions: use
versus occupation, application to private actors, and the relationship between resource
extraction and appropriation. Traces the legislative history of Title IV from the 2014
ASTEROIDS Act through H.R. 1508 to enactment. Argues, using W. Michael Reisman's
"international incidents" framework, that domestic legislation such as Title IV functions
as a State interpretation that helps fill gaps in an ambiguous treaty regime rather than
as a violation of it, and proposes that future international stability in space resource
activities is more likely to come from technical/safety-standard coordination (on the
ITU/ICAO model) than from resolving sovereignty questions directly.

## Summary

### Background and objective

The article responds to a wave of commentary, published in late 2015 (cited from Miami New
Times, The Conversation, CBC News, and SpaceNews), that characterized the newly passed
CSLCA as an extraterritorial land grab and an assault on settled principles of space law
that violated Article II of the Outer Space Treaty. The authors set out to test that claim
by examining whether Article II's text actually forecloses the property-rights scheme
Title IV creates, or whether Article II is ambiguous enough that Title IV can instead be
read as a legitimate, if contestable, State interpretation of the treaty.

The authors' stated organizing premise is that the Outer Space Treaty was drafted during
Cold War negotiations to be deliberately broad, leaving States considerable room to
negotiate the specific content of its principles so the law could adapt as space
technology developed, and that this open texture is itself a value embedded in the treaty
rather than a defect to be resolved by unilateral declaration of a single fixed meaning
for Article II. The article frames Article II as best read neither as a socialist
(communitarian) nor a purely liberal (free-use) provision, but as an anti-imperial/anti-
colonial compromise between those traditions, aimed at excluding the extension of
terrestrial territorial claims into space.

The paper is structured in four parts: Part I catalogs three specific ambiguities within
Article II; Part II summarizes Title IV's legislative development and gives a surface-
level compliance analysis; Part III develops a jurisprudential argument for why domestic
legislation can help constitute the content of international law and applies that argument
to Title IV; Part IV considers what an international regime for space resource activities
might look like if Title IV's interpretation gains acceptance.

### Methods and scope

The article is a doctrinal legal analysis; it does not present original empirical data.
Its methodology consists of (1) close textual reading of Article I, II, VI, VIII, IX, and
XII of the Outer Space Treaty and comparison with related instruments (the Moon Agreement,
the 1961 UN General Assembly resolution on international cooperation in outer space, the
Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties' interpretive rules); (2) legislative history
review of the ASTEROIDS Act (H.R. 5063, 113th Cong., 2014), H.R. 1508 (Space Resources
Exploration and Utilization Act of 2015), and Title IV of the CSLCA (H.R. 2262, 114th
Cong., enacted as Pub. L. No. 114-90, 129 Stat. 704, § 402); (3) comparison of the outer-
space non-appropriation regime with analogous "global commons" regimes — the high seas,
the deep seabed, and Antarctica — to test whether resource extraction is generally treated
as compatible with non-appropriation in those regimes; (4) application of a
jurisprudential theory (W. Michael Reisman's "international incident" / "epistemic unit"
model, and secondary literature on "soft law" in space governance) to argue for how
ambiguous treaty content is filled in practice; and (5) discussion of one contemporaneous
case, *Nemitz v. United States* (D. Nev. 2004, aff'd 9th Cir. 2005), as an illustration of
the private-actor ambiguity.

The scope is limited to Article II's non-appropriation principle and its intersection with
commercial resource extraction; it does not analyze other Title IV provisions unrelated to
resources (the CSLCA also amended other areas of U.S. commercial space law, which the
article notes only in passing as riders that were substantively unconnected to
extraterrestrial resource issues).

### Key findings

- **What Title IV does.** Title IV's operative clause (CSLCA § 402, codified from H.R. 2262)
  entitles a U.S. citizen who commercially recovers an asteroid resource or space resource
  to possess, own, transport, use, and sell what was obtained, subject to applicable law
  including the international obligations of the United States. The Act defines two
  resource categories, asteroid resources and space resources, with space resources
  further specified to include water and minerals. The authors characterize this as
  granting an enumerated subset of the traditional chattel-property bundle of rights to
  extracted materials, rather than granting generalized property rights outright, and read
  this as narrower and more defensible than the language of its legislative predecessors.

- **Legislative lineage.** The property-rights concept originated in the 2014 ASTEROIDS Act
  (H.R. 5063), which declared without qualification that resources obtained from an
  asteroid become the property of the entity that obtained them. Because that bill did not
  define outer space resources, the authors note it was read by some as capable of
  supporting expansive claims. A 2015 letter from commentators Berin Szoka and James
  Dunstan to members of Congress argued the successor bill, H.R. 1508, could be read to
  permit expansive territorial claims over both asteroids and planetary surfaces, while
  simultaneously being too narrow because it limited property rights to asteroid-derived
  resources only. Title IV, as finally enacted, was folded into the larger CSLCA and
  signed by President Obama on November 25, 2015.

- **The sovereignty disclaimer.** Unlike its predecessor bills, Title IV as enacted adds
  language, described by the authors as new, expressly stating that the Act does not
  thereby assert sovereignty, sovereign or exclusive rights, jurisdiction, or ownership
  over any celestial body. The article treats this disclaimer as textually significant
  evidence that Congress drafted with Article II compliance in mind.

- **A reporting requirement, not a completed regulatory scheme.** Title IV also directs the
  President to prepare a report identifying the authorities needed to meet the
  international obligations of the United States, including authorization and continuing
  supervision by the federal government. The authors read this as showing Title IV is not
  a final settlement even of U.S. domestic law on the subject, since the actual
  authorization/supervision framework required by Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty was
  left to future action.

- **Three Article II ambiguities identified.** (1) *Use and occupation*: Article II bars
  appropriation of outer space through sovereignty claims, use, occupation, or comparable
  means, but Article I affirms a right of exploration and use, and Article XII
  contemplates reciprocal access to installations on celestial bodies — meaning occupation
  as such is not barred, only occupation that amounts to a sovereignty claim. (2) *Private
  actors*: Article II does not name private parties, and the authors describe scholarship
  as split between an extended reading that treats a State grant of private property
  rights as a functional act of appropriation, and a reading that treats Article II as
  inapplicable to individuals altogether; the article's own position is that Article VI,
  which makes non-governmental activity attributable to the sponsoring State, is the
  mechanism that extends Article II's constraints to private actors, without imposing an
  international legal obligation on the individual directly. (3) *Resource exploitation as
  appropriation*: the authors report that Article II's text contains no explicit
  prohibition on extracting and appropriating natural resources, citing one source's view
  that the treaty does not forbid extraction and appropriation of resources, while also
  noting the contrary position (citing Stephen Gorove) that consuming or taking resources
  with the intent of keeping them for exclusive use amounts to appropriation.

- **Territory versus property distinction.** The article's central doctrinal move is that
  Article II's non-appropriation principle governs claims of territorial sovereignty, not
  property as such, and that appropriation in the treaty sense is a spatial/territorial
  concept inherited from the post-1945 international legal order, drawing on Carl
  Schmitt's account of land appropriation as a foundational act of law-making. Under this
  reading, resource extraction only implicates Article II if it functions as a proxy for a
  territorial claim.

- **Comparative global-commons analysis.** The article compares treatment of resource
  extraction under three other global-commons regimes: the high seas are described as an
  area of broadly liberal usage permitting extraction (citing UNCLOS art. 87); the deep
  seabed's mineral resources are governed by an international authority (UNCLOS arts.
  136-37, 156); and commercial mineral exploitation in Antarctica is prohibited outright
  (Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty, art. 7). The Moon
  Agreement's unresolved attempt to impose a deep-seabed-style international authority on
  lunar resources (art. XI) is cited as a precedent that failed to gain broad
  ratification. The authors conclude that resource extraction is not inherently
  incompatible with commons status, and that outer space's lex specialis simply lacks the
  specific extraction clause the other regimes have.

- **Nemitz v. United States.** The article recounts this case as an example of the private-
  actor ambiguity: Gregory Nemitz claimed ownership of an asteroid and attempted to charge
  NASA rent for a spacecraft occupying it, arguing the Outer Space Treaty binds only
  States and not him as an individual. The authors describe the claim as far-fetched on
  its facts but use it to frame the underlying doctrinal question of how treaty
  obligations reach private conduct.

- **Reisman's international-incidents / epistemic-unit framework.** The article adopts legal
  scholar W. Michael Reisman's account (1984, Yale Journal of International Law) that
  international law's content is built incrementally at decision points where
  practitioners interpret and apply ambiguous law, comparable to common-law adjudication,
  and extends this to argue domestic legislation like Title IV is itself an epistemic unit
  that States use to propose content for ambiguous treaty terms — comparable, per the
  article, to how non-discriminatory-access language migrated from U.S. domestic remote-
  sensing law into UN Principles on Remote Sensing, and to how State reactions to the 2007
  Chinese and 2008 U.S. anti-satellite tests helped clarify the scope of Article IX's ban
  on harmful interference.

- **Precedent framing: sovereignty disclaimed, resources kept.** The authors point to the
  plaque left by a U.S. Apollo mission (the text names Apollo 12 in the body; footnote 89
  cites the Apollo 11 plaque, an internal inconsistency in the source) disclaiming
  sovereignty while the United States nonetheless retained ownership of returned lunar
  samples, framing this as an existing precedent of use without territorial claim, paired
  with resource extraction and retained ownership, that Title IV extends to private
  commercial actors.

- **No settlement claimed; no diplomatic reaction reported.** The article explicitly states
  it does not argue Title IV constitutes international law by itself, only that it
  represents the United States' own understanding of its obligations under Article II,
  leaving other States to accept, reject, or ignore that interpretation. As of the
  article's writing, the authors report that no other State had issued a formal diplomatic
  objection to Title IV.

- **A harmful-interference gap acknowledged.** The authors flag one specific compliance risk
  Title IV leaves open: it contains no explicit provision preventing a private entity that
  has lawfully extracted resources from one part of a body from asserting an Article IX
  harmful-interference claim against a competing operator on the same body, which could
  function as a de facto exclusive claim over that location.

- **Proposed path forward: technical/safety coordination over sovereignty resolution.** Part
  IV argues international stability is more likely to emerge from technical safety-
  standard and information-sharing coordination — on the model of the International
  Telecommunication Union (ITU) and International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) —
  than from States directly litigating the limits of sovereignty in space. As a concrete
  example of a U.S. domestic standard migrating internationally, the article cites the
  maximum-probable-loss insurance standard for launch liability, originally a U.S.
  innovation, subsequently adopted or adapted by Australia, Korea, and France.

- **Concluding assessment.** The authors state plainly that most companies positioned to
  exploit the new provisions are, in their words, "still decks of PowerPoint slides
  seeking funding," and that actual resource-extraction activity is likely decades away.
  They predict the Article II/Title IV debate will be settled by international practice
  over time rather than by the U.S. legislation alone, and note (citing a 2014 paper by
  Anita Rinner) that Austria's national mining law has been proposed elsewhere as a
  possible model for developing extraction frameworks compatible with Article II.

### Limitations

The article is doctrinal/interpretive legal scholarship, not empirical research; it
presents no original data set, survey, or quantitative analysis, and its conclusions about
likely international reception are explicitly predictive and untested at the time of
writing (the authors themselves note the absence of any diplomatic reaction to evaluate).
The analysis centers on U.S. legislative history and a U.S.-authored legal argument;
treatment of how other spacefaring States interpret Article II is limited to citing
secondary commentary rather than analyzing foreign legislation or diplomatic practice in
comparable depth. The comparative global-commons analysis (high seas, deep seabed,
Antarctica) is presented as illustrative rather than as a rigorous functional-equivalence
test, and the authors acknowledge the high-seas fishing analogy in particular has limited
power to establish specific legal principles. The article also does not resolve, and does
not claim to resolve, whether Title IV is the single correct interpretation of Article II
— only that it is a plausible one; the authors state this distinction explicitly. Two
internal inconsistencies appear in the source itself and are reproduced neutrally above
rather than silently corrected: the Apollo 11/Apollo 12 plaque citation, and the
Robison/Robinson author-name spelling.

### Topic mapping

FA4. Source list entry 2. Sub-Q 3. This source addresses: the non-appropriation principle
of Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty and its interaction with Articles I, VI, VIII,
IX, and XII; the legislative history and statutory text of Title IV of the U.S. Commercial
Space Launch Competitiveness Act of 2015 (space resource property rights, the definitions
of asteroid resource and space resource, the sovereignty-disclaimer clause, and the
presidential reporting requirement); comparative treatment of resource extraction under
other global-commons legal regimes (high seas/UNCLOS, deep seabed, Antarctica, the Moon
Agreement); private-actor liability and jurisdiction questions in space law, including the
*Nemitz v. United States* litigation; jurisprudential theory on how domestic legislation and
soft law contribute to the formation of customary/interpretive international law (Reisman's
international-incidents framework); and proposals for international coordination mechanisms
(technical safety standards, information-sharing regimes analogous to ITU/ICAO practice, the
maximum-probable-loss insurance standard) as an alternative to direct resolution of
sovereignty questions in outer space resource governance.
